title: Opinion No. 9/2025 (China)
body: UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention
attribution: Opinions adopted by the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention, published by OHCHR (ohchr.org). United Nations documents.
text:
Human Rights Council
Working Group on Arbitrary Detention
  Opinions adopted by the Working Group on Arbitrary
Detention at its 102nd session, 1–10 April 2025
  Opinion No. 9/2025 concerning Ji Xiaolong and Chen Pinlin (China)
1. The Working Group on Arbitrary Detention was established in resolution 1991/42 of
the Commission on Human Rights. In its resolution 1997/50, the Commission extended and
clarified the mandate of the Working Group. Pursuant to General Assembly resolution 60/251
and Human Rights Council decision 1/102, the Council assumed the mandate of th e
Commission. The Council most recently extended the mandate of the Working Group for a
three-year period in its resolution 51/8.
2. In accordance with its methods of work ,1 on 25 November 2024 the Working Group
transmitted to the Government of China a communication concerning Ji Xiaolong and Chen
Pinlin. The Government replied to the communication on 25 November 2024. The State is
not a party to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights.
3. The Working Group regards deprivation of liberty as arbitrary in the following cases:
 (a) When it is clearly impossible to invoke any legal basis justifying the
deprivation of liberty (as when a person is kept in detention after the completion of his or her
sentence or despite an amnesty law applicable to him or her) (category I);
 (b) When the deprivation of liberty results from the exercise of the rights or
freedoms guaranteed by articles 7, 13, 14, 18, 19, 20 and 21 of the Universal Declaration of
Human Rights and, insofar as States parties are concerned, by articles 12, 18, 19, 21, 22, 25,
26 and 27 of the Covenant (category II);
 (c) When the total or partial non-observance of the international norms relating to
the right to a fair trial, established in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and in the
relevant international instruments accepted by the States concerned, is of such gravity as to
give the deprivation of liberty an arbitrary character (category III);
 (d) When asylum -seekers, immigrants or refugees are subjected to prolonged
administrative custody without the possibility of administrative or judicial review or remedy
(category IV);
 (e) When the deprivation of liberty constitutes a violation of international law on
the grounds of discrimination , based on birth, national, ethnic or social origin, language,
religion, economic condition, political or other opinion, gender, sexual orientation, disability
or any other status, that aims towards or can result in ignoring the equality of human beings
(category V).

 1 A/HRC/36/38.

 A/HRC/WGAD/2025/9
 Advance edited version Distr.: General
29 May 2025

Original: English

A/HRC/WGAD/2025/9
2
 1. Submissions
 (a) Communication from the source
4. Ji Xiaolong is a citizen of China, born in 1976. His usual place of residence is in
Pudong New District, Shanghai.
5. The source submits that Mr. Ji is a prominent human rights defender and an online
commentator. Before he became involved in human rights advocacy, he founded and ran a
business in Shanghai. Mr. Ji is also a Christian.
6. Chen Pinlin is a citizen of China, born in 1991. His usual place of residence is in
Baoshan District, Shanghai.
7. Mr. Chen was the manager of the Shanghai Xinfei Media Company, and, like Mr. Ji,
also an online commentator, who used the screenname “Plato”.
 (i) Arrest and detention of Mr. Ji
8. The source reports that in 2015, Mr. Ji was summoned by Shanghai police for “picking
quarrels and provoking trouble ” for writing articles online about democracy and
constitutionalism and was given 15 days’ administrative detention as a punishment, which is
believed to be when he started to become even more involved in human rights advocacy.
9. Between 2018 and 2022, Mr. Ji spent three and a half  years in prison on charges of
“picking quarrels and provoking trouble ” for his “toilet revolution ” campaign. The source
states that after the leader of China gave a speech in 2018 about improving public bathroom
facilities, Mr. Ji wrote slogans criticizing the country ’s leadership and the Communist Party
in various public sanitary facilities.
10. According to the source, Mr. Ji was detained in July 2018 and held under “residential
surveillance in a designat ed location” – a form of de facto enforced disappearance. He was
tried and convicted in January 2019. Mr. Ji served his sentence in Shanghai City ’s
Baimaoling Prison, where the source submits that he faced torture and other forms of ill -
treatment. Mr. Ji was released in February 2022, at the end of his sentence.
11. Most recently, Mr. Ji was arrested again on 31 August 2022 at his home in Pudong
New District, Shanghai, at around 3.30 p.m., by officers from Meiyuan New Village Police
Station which comes under the Pudong New District Branch of the Shanghai Public Security
Bureau.
12. The arresting authorities did not show a warrant when arresting Mr . Ji. On
2 September 2022, his partner was told verbally that he had been criminally detained, and his
parents, who live 130 km away in Jiangsu Province, received a written criminal detention
notice on 4 September 2022. The authority issuing the arrest notice was the Pudong New
District Branch of the Shanghai Public Security Bureau.
13. The reason given for his arrest was “picking quarrels and provoking trouble”. Article
293 of the Criminal Law of China, which defines “picking quarrels and provoking trouble ”,
prescribes a fixed-term imprisonment of up to five years for those who: (a) wilfully attack
another person , where the circumstances are serious; ( b) chase, intercept or curs e another
person, where the circumstances are serious; (c) forcibly take or demand, or wilfully damage
or occupy public or private property , where  the circumstances are serious; or ( d) create a
disturbance in a public place, causing serious disorder.
14. The source submits that Mr. Ji has been in continuous detention since 31 August 2022.
He was formally arrested on 23 September 2022 and indicted on 17 March 2023. On 27
October 2023, Mr. Ji was convicted and sentenced to four years and six months in priso n.
15. The source notes that the Shanghai Pudong New District Procuratorate ordered Mr.
Ji’s arrest and indictment and the Shanghai Pudong New District People ’s Court ordered his
custodial sentence.
16. Mr. Ji appealed against his four-and-a-half-year prison sentence. The hearing was held
on 17 March 2024 at Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People ’s Court. During the hearing, Mr.
Ji read out a statement, in which he alleged that the persecution against him had never stopped

A/HRC/WGAD/2025/9
 3
since the investigation began. He was reportedly not given glasses, books to read or dental
treatment in the detention centre, and his basic rights were not protected. It was argued that
his arrest was entirely due to his appeal to officials to protect the  people’s rights during the
pandemic and his open letter to the Premier of China. The judge interrupted Mr.  Ji’s
statement. On 17 April 2024, the Court rejected Mr. Ji’s appeal.
17. The source report that Mr. Ji is currently detained in ward 8 at Shanghai New Prison
in Shanghai. He had previously been detained in the Pudong New District Detention Centre,
also located in Shanghai. The source notes that the authorities do not notify the families of
the exact transfer date before an individual is moved to a prison. Mr. Ji’s family was notified
on 9 June 2024 that he had already arrived at Shanghai New Prison, and therefore it is
believed that he was moved in early June 2024.
18. The source submits that on 14 November 2022, more than 115 supporters of Mr. Ji
signed an open letter urging authorities to improve the situation for Mr. Ji in detention,
including with regard to the overcrowding and the lack of dental treatment. The source regrets
that their open letter did not result in an improvement in the conditions of his detention.
 (ii) Arrest and detention of Mr. Chen
19. The source submits that on 28 November 2023, Mr. Chen was arrested at his home in
Shanghai by officials from the Baoshan Branch of the Shanghai Municipal Public Security
Bureau. At 11.50 p.m. on that day, the police came to Mr. Chen ’s residence and summoned
him with a search warrant.
20. According to the source, the police had cautioned those present at the time of
Mr. Chen’s arrest not to speak publicly about his arrest, and further stated that they were only
taking him away for questioning, and that talking about it would harm his case.
21. The reason for the arrest imputed by the authorities is, as in Mr. Ji ’s case, “picking
quarrels and provoking trouble” – an offence set forth in article 293 of the Criminal Law.
22. The source submits that Mr. Chen has been in continuous detention since
28 November 2023, having been criminally detained on 29 November 2023. The detention
was ordered by the Shanghai Baoshan District People ’s Procuratorate. Mr. Chen was
formally arrested on 5 January 2024 and indicted on 3 April 2024. He is being held at the
Baoshan District Detention Centre in Shanghai.
23. The source specifies that Mr. Chen has not yet been presented before a judge , as the
trial has not yet commenced. Under the Criminal Procedure Law, the police may apply to the
Procuratorate to approve the arrest warrant. The Procuratorate then files the indictment
charge against the defendant. Judges are only involved in the trials.
24. The source submits that Mr. Chen was able to meet his lawyer for the first time one
month after his apprehension, on 27 December 2023. He met with his current legal counsel
on 8 February 2024. The first lawyer has since relocated abroad, and therefore is no longer
representing Mr. Chen. Both the current and former lawyers were of Mr. Chen’s choosing.
 (iii) Legal analysis concerning Mr. Ji
25. The source submits that the detention of Mr. Ji is in violation of his right to peacefully
exercise freedom of expression, and of rights guaranteed under articles 9, 10, 12, 18, 19, 21,
22 and 26 of the Covenant and articles 9, 10, 18, 19 and 20 of the Universal Declaration of
Human Rights, and falls under categories II and III of the Working Group.
26. With regard to category II, the source notes that Mr. Ji has been convicted and
sentenced to four years and six months in prison on charges that are tied to his exercise of his
right to freedom of expression online.
27. During the spring of 2022, the authorities in Shanghai instituted a strict coronavirus
disease (COVID-19) lockdown that lasted approximately two months and reportedly caused
numerous limitations on economic and social rights. According to the source, these measures
particularly affected vulnerable groups, such as migrant workers and those with pre-existing
medical conditions.

A/HRC/WGAD/2025/9
4
28. After Mr. Ji was released from prison , having completed a three-and-a-half-year
sentence in February 2022, he began to speak out online about these lockdown measures. On
2 April 2022, Mr. Ji posted a “citizen’s petition” on WeChat and Twitter (now X) that called
on the Government to stop its restrictive pandemic measures. As a result, his WeChat account
was blocked. On 4 April 2022, Mr. Ji published an open letter  addressed to “All Public
Officials” on his Twitter account , which had nearly 32,000 followers, and the next day he
gave an interview to a foreign media outlet about his  online criticism of the Government ’s
pandemic measures.
29. On 30 April 2022, Mr. Ji was briefly detained at Meiyuan New Village Police Station
on suspicion of “picking quarrels and provoking trouble ” and was then released on bail the
next day. On that occasion, the police confiscated his phone, ID card and passport. Mr. Ji
continued to post comments online on his Twitter account between April 2022 and his
detention in August 2022. Police officers and national security officers took him away briefly
for questioning several times, including on 29 May 2022, 4 June 2022 and 23 August 2022.
30. On 29 August 2022, Mr. Ji posted an open letter on Twitter criticizing Shanghai ’s
then Party Secretary, who became the Premier of China in March 2023, call ing on him to
step down and take accountability for the difficult humanitarian situation caused by the
lockdown. The letter also reiterated his opposition to the top leadership of China and
criticized it for its ambition to amend the Constitution. The letter stated that the police would
not allow him to go back to his home  town to take care of his eld erly family members and
obtain his social insurance card. Mr. Ji created his open letter as a  non-fungible token so it
could not be censored and would “always exist” online. The source recalls that it is in this
context, two days after issuing th e open letter, was Mr. Ji taken away from his home and
criminally detained on charges of “picking quarrels and provoking trouble”.
31. The source submits that the investigation focused on Mr. Ji ’s comments about the
pandemic measures, which the police were treating as acts of spreading rumours, and that
Mr. Ji was suspected of insulting national leaders.
32. On 17 March 2023, Mr. Ji was indicted by the Shanghai Pudong New District
Procuratorate. The indictment stated that from April to August 2022, Mr. Ji had published or
forwarded a large amount of false information that seriously damaged the country ’s image,
on the overseas social media platform Twitter. At the time of the incident, Mr. Ji ’s Twitter
account had 31,217 followers. On 30 April 2022, he was arrested by the police , and refused
to confess to the facts of the crime. He had also published or forwarded a large amount of
false information many times while he was out on bail awaiting trial in this case.
33. While the indictment did not mention the COVID -19 pandemic or specifics about
what content posted by Mr. Ji  was “false”, it made clear that his online expression was the
reason for his detention, notes the source.
34. The Shanghai Pudong New District People ’s Court commenced Mr. Ji ’s trial on
21 June 2023, and convicted him on 27 October 2023 on charges of “picking quarrels and
provoking trouble”, sentencing him to four years and six months in prison. The Court stated
that Mr. Ji  had “spread a large amount of false information on overseas social networks,
instigated trouble, and confused the public”, though again it did not cite any specific content.
The Court also stated that Mr. Ji was a “repeat offender” and therefore “should be punished
more severely according to law ”. The source notes in this regard that article 65 of the
Criminal Law provides for further punitive measures for recidivists convicted within five
years of completing their sentences.
35. Regarding category III, the source submits that the overall circumstances demonstrate
multiple violations of Mr. Ji’s right to a fair trial, guaranteed under articles 9 of the Covenant
and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
36. In this regard, the source notes that Mr. Ji was subjected to procedural violations of
his legal rights from the moment of detention to the court proceedings.  Firstly, the source
recalls that the police did not show a warrant when detaining Mr. Ji on 31 August 2022, in
violation of article 85 of the Criminal Procedure Law. Further more, Mr. Ji’s family did not
receive the detention notice until 4 September 2022, even though the family must reportedly
be notified within 24 hours under the same provision. The source notes that while there are

A/HRC/WGAD/2025/9
 5
exceptions to article 85, none applied in Mr. Ji’s case (e.g. Mr. Ji was not held on national
security or terrorist charges, notification would not obstruct the investigation, and it did not
seem that it was impossible to notify the family as they were notified within a week).
37. The source further submits that the authorities also deprived Mr. Ji of access to his
legal counsel for longer than 48 hours after such request was made, which is the limit set for
a non-national security crime under article 39 of the Criminal Procedure Law.
38. Moreover, the source alleges  that Mr. Ji is deprived of his liberty in inhumane
conditions in the detention centre and that his complaints about medical treatment were
ignored. Mr. Ji is reportedly suffering from untreated dental issues, the cells were very
crowded, and his family ’s packages were rejected due to pandemic measures. He was only
allowed to shower once a week.
39. The source reports that the room in the detention centre where Mr. Ji was held could
only accommodate 25 people, but because there were many prisoners, it held more than
60 people. Inmates reportedly could not lie down when sleeping, nor could they flex their
extremities. Mr. Ji ’s toothache had become very severe and his requests for treatment were
being ignored.
40. On 26 April 2023, Mr. Ji ’s lawyer visited Mr. Ji in detention. The lawyer was
reportedly not permitted to read Mr. Ji ’s case files, in violation of article 40 of the Criminal
Procedure Law which allows lawyers to read, copy and reproduce case files after the case
has been transferred to the Procuratorate for review. Mr. Ji had already been indicted  on
17 March 2023 by the Procuratorate.
41. The trial of Mr. Ji took place  on 21 June 2023 at the Shanghai Pudong New District
Court. Mr. Ji was only told about the hearing in the morning o n 21 June 2023. The source
submits that this constitutes a violation of article 187 of the Criminal Procedure Law , which
states that trial summons should be sent at least three days in advance. Mr. Ji reportedly raised
concerns about the violation of his rights with the judge but was ignored.
42. The materials that Mr. Ji had prepared for his defence were reportedly confiscated by
the detention centre and he was not allowed to bring them with him to the court. Mr. Ji ’s
defence lawyer asked the court to postpone the hearing but the request was denied.
43. The source further submits that Mr. Ji ’s trial was closed to the public and that only
two members of his family were allowed to attend the hearing. In addition, there were no
witnesses present during the court proceedings.
44. The source submits that Mr. Ji was subjected to prolonged interrogation, was forced
to sit in an iron chair for extended periods and was handcuffed. Furthermore, Mr. Ji’s defence
team had reportedly requested the footage of the interrogation, but the authorities did not
provide it, stating that the interrogation records might not be used as evidence. Mr.  Ji’s
appearance had drastically changed since before his detention: his hair had turned partially
white, and he had become extremely thin.
45. Mr. Ji’s defence lawyers requested the court to exclude unlawfully obtained evidence
– the statements made by Mr. Ji  – as they had reportedly been made under duress and
following ill-treatment. The source reports  that the prosecution and the court agreed to
exclude these statements, and they were not presented during the trial.
46. The source notes that article 56 of the Criminal Procedure Law stipulates that
“criminal suspects ’ or defendants ’ confessions gathered by the use of torture to extract
confessions, or other illegal methods, or witness testimony or victim statements gathered by
the use of illegal methods such as violence or threats, shall be excluded ”.
47. In early June 2024, Mr. Ji was transferred to Shanghai New Prison. Mr. Ji ’s family’s
application for a visit had still not been approved. Prison officials said that the public security
officer in charge of the case needed to agree before issuing a visit notice. The source reports
that Mr. Ji’s right to family remains breached, in violation of article 48 of the Prison Law.

A/HRC/WGAD/2025/9
6
 (iv) Legal analysis concerning Mr. Chen
48. The source submits that the detention of Mr. Chen also falls under categories II and III
of the Working Group.
49. In regard to category II, the source argues that Mr. Chen’s detention is in violation of
the right to peacefully exercise freedom of expression  as guaranteed by the Covenant and
under articles 18, 19 and 20 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The source
submits that the detention of Mr. Chen is due to his exercise of his right to freedom of
expression online.
50. In this context, the source notes  that on 26 November 2022 Mr. Chen attended and
filmed a protest in Shanghai. The protest reportedly broke out in response to a fire in the city
of Urumqi, Xinjiang U ighur Autonomous Region, two days earlier, during which several
residents reportedly died after not being able to escape due to strict COVID -19 lockdown
measures. Many Shanghai residents had gathered on Urumqi Middle Road in Shanghai. The
protesters chanted slogans, including ones that called on the country ’s authorities to resign.
Some of these protesters were detained. The source reports that the protest in Shanghai was
one of the first in a wider protest movement across the country, which was later called the
“White Paper Protests” or “White Paper Movement”.
51. Mr. Chen reportedly compiled footage of this protest into a documentary called
“Urumqi Middle Road”, which he released on YouTube on 27 November 2023, near the one-
year anniversary of the protests. He also posted the video on his accounts on X (formerly
Twitter), Reddit and Telegram.
52. The source recalls that one day after posting this video online, on 28 November 2023,
Mr. Chen was detained on suspicion of “picking quarrels and provoking trouble”. Mr. Chen’s
family was unable to find a lawyer to take on his case until mid -December 2023, due to the
sensitivity of the case. On 5 January 2024, Mr. Chen was formally arrested on charges of
“picking quarrels and provoking trouble ”. On 18 February 2024, his case was transferred to
the Procuratorate’s office for prosecution. On 3 April 2024, he was indicted by the Shanghai
Baoshan District Procuratorate.
53. The indictment states that the reason for Mr. Chen’s arrest was that he had produced
and published online a documentary video. It states that Mr. Chen used his mobile phone to
shoot and save live video of the incident on Urumqi Middle Road in Shanghai on the evening
of 26 November 2022. He later used it for the purposes of expressing dissatisfaction with the
epidemic prevention and control policies , and of driving traffic to overseas social media
platforms to seek economic benefits. The indictment further states that i n September 2023,
Mr. Chen began to produce the “Urumqi Middle Road Documentary on the First Anniversary
of the White Paper Movement ”, using  YouTube video software. It was completed on 27
November 2023. Mr. Chen promoted it through multiple overseas social media platforms,
such as Twitter, Telegram and Reddit, causing the “documentary” to quickly spread on the
overseas Internet, garnering up to 210,000 Twitter “likes”. Much of the content of this
documentary was false and Mr. Chen knowingly spread fabricated information, causing
serious disrupti on to public order; and the documentar y quoted insulting remarks about
national leaders, damaging the country’s image and seriously endangering national interests.
54. The source reiterates that the indictment clearly states that Mr. Chen is being
prosecuted for posting a compilation of video clips online, some that he shot himself and
others from reputable international media outlets. The source submits that to describe the
footage as fabricated information is false. The footage included clips of protesters chanting
slogans calling for the authorities to step down , which resulted in the accusation against
Mr. Chen of insulting national leaders. During interrogations by the police, Mr. Chen stated
that he himself did not chant these slogans. The source recalls that article 35 of the
Constitution of the People’s Republic of China protects the right to freedom of speech.
55. In relation to category III, the source submits that Mr. Chen has been denied the right
to a fair trial.
56. In this regard, the source notes that Mr. Chen has not been brought before a judge and
that only the public security bureau and prosecutors have reviewed the case details and

A/HRC/WGAD/2025/9
 7
evidence against him, in violation of international human rights standards. On 7 June 2024,
the hearing was cancelled on the grounds that the court needed more time.
57. One of Mr. Chen ’s lawyers applied for bail, but it was rejected on the grounds that
Mr. Chen might “form a gang to commit a crime ” and in order to “prevent Mr. Chen from
colluding with others to fabricate testimony”.
58. The source submits that these arguments of the court do not conform with the case
facts and appear to be designed to keep Mr. Chen in custody on the grounds permitted under
article 82 of the Criminal Procedure Law.
59. The source points out that under international human rights standards, detention in
custody should be a last resort under the principle of the presumption of innocence.
60. Furthermore, lawyers have reportedly not been allowed to copy the electronic data
from Mr. Chen ’s mobile phone and his computer , which is being used as evidence against
him. This data includes text, audio, and the promotional video that he made for the
documentary. The source argues that the lack of access to this data hinders Mr. Chen’s ability
to mount a defence, as is guaranteed under international law. It also violates article 40 of the
Criminal Procedure Law , in which it is stated that “from the day that the People ’s
Procuratorate begins reviewing for prosecution, defence lawyers may read, copy and
reproduce case file materials ”. Other national judicial procedures reportedly state that the
copying of case files may be done by photocopying, photographing, scanning, electronic data
copying and so on.
61. On 16 August 2024, Mr. Chen’s lawyers filed a complaint with the Second Branch of
the Shanghai People’s Procuratorate over the decision of the judge at the Shanghai Baoshan
District People’s Court to deny the defence lawyers’ right to review evidence.
62. Despite the ongoing denial of the defence lawyers ’ right to copy case evidence in
order to mount a defence, the Shanghai Baoshan District People ’s Court arranged for a
pretrial meeting to be held on 16 August 2024. The two defence lawyers attended it, even
though it was held in violation of domestic procedural rules that the defence lawyers should
have access to all case materials before the pretrial meeting.
63. The source further submits that since a defendant should be presumed innocent until
proven guilty, the ongoing denial of communication to his family hinders Mr. Chen’s rights.
64. It is submitted that the crime Mr. Ji was convicted of and indicted for, namely “picking
quarrels and provoking trouble ”, stipulated under article 293 of the Criminal Law, has
repeatedly been used by authorities since 2013 to punish forms of online expression protected
under international law.
65. In this context, the source recalls that a judicial interpretation issued on 10 September
2013 by the Supreme People ’s Court and the  Supreme People ’s Procuratorate stated that
anyone who fabricates false information, knowingly spreads false information, or organizes
or instigates others to spread false information online is to be punished under article 293 (4)
of the Criminal Law. The source submits that this provision is so vague and overly broad that
nearly any expression can fall under the definition of “creating a disturbance in a public place,
causing serious disorder”.
66. The source submits that this criminal provision has repeatedly  been used to target
human rights defenders, lawyers, writers and others for their online expression. It further
recalls that the Working Group has in the past considered the crime of “picking quarrels and
provoking trouble” and other charges to be “so vague and overly broad that it was impossible
to invoke a legal basis justifying the deprivation of liberty ”.2
67. The source further notes that there have been growing calls in China for reform of the
crime of “picking quarrels and provoking trouble ”. A survey published in 2023 and
conducted by the Supreme People’s Court in two provinces found that the charge was being
overused.

 2 See, for example, opinion No. 62/2018, para. 58.

A/HRC/WGAD/2025/9
8
 (b) Response from the Government
68. On 25 November 2024, the Working Group transmitted the allegations from the
source to the Government of China under its regular communications procedure. The
Working Group requested the Government to provide it, by 27 January 2025, with detailed
information about Mr. Ji and Mr. Chen and to clarify the legal provisions justifying their
continued detention, as well as its compatibility with the obligations of China under
international human rights law. Moreover, the Working Group call ed upon the Government
of China to ensure their physical and mental integrity.
69. On 25 November 2024, the Government submitted its reply. The Government stated
that Mr. Ji is a 48-year-old male. In order to vent his dissatisfaction, Mr. Ji repeatedly caused
disturbances in public places in July 2018, disrupting social order and  causing serious
disorder in public places. His behavio ur constituted the crime of picking  quarrels and
provoking trouble. On 14 January 2019 , the People ’s Court in Pudong New  District,
Shanghai, sentenced Mr. Ji to three years and six months in prison for the crime of  picking
quarrels and provoking trouble. After the sentencing, Mr. Li filed an appeal. The  Shanghai
First Intermediate People’s Court, after hearing the case in accordance with the law, rejected
the appeal and upheld the original ruling, on 11 April 2019.
70. After Mr. Ji  was released from prison, he fabricated a large amount of false
information and spread  it on information networks from April to August 2022, seriously
disrupting public order. His actions constituted the crime of picking quarrels and provoking
trouble. As a repeat offender, he was subject to severe penalties, in accordance with the law.
On 14 October 2023, the People’s Court in Pudong New District, Shanghai, sentenced Mr. Ji
to four years and six months in prison for the crime of picking quarrels and provoking trouble.
After the sentencing, Mr. Ji filed an appeal. The Shanghai First Intermediate People’s Court,
after hearing the case in accordance with the law, rejected the appeal and upheld the original
ruling, on 17 April 2024. Mr. Ji is currently serving time in prison.
71. Mr. Chen is a 33 -year-old male. In November 2023, he was placed in criminal
detention by the Shanghai public security bodies, in accordance with the law, on suspicion
of picking quarrels and provoking trouble. On 3 April 2024, he was prosecuted by the
Baoshan District People’s Procuratorate in Shanghai. The case was postponed because the
accused changed defence counsel. The Baoshan District People ’s Court in Shanghai will set
a date to hear this case.
72. China is a country ruled by law, and the judicial bodies have protected the legitimate
rights of Mr. Ji and Mr. Chen, in accordance with the law. The country’s prisons have always
enforced the law adhering to strict, fair and civilized standards, guaranteed the rights of
prisoners to life, health, visits and correspondence in accordance with the law and accepted
the legal supervision of the people’s procuratorates.
 (c) Further comments from the source
73. The Government’s reply was sent to the source for further comments on 26 November
2024, which the source submitted on 9 December 2024. In further comments, regarding Mr.
Ji, the source noted that his convictions in 2019 and 2023 both stem from his exercise of the
right to freedom of expression. His peaceful actions – writing slogans critical of the country’s
leadership in public restrooms and posting online commentaries urging the Government to
lift restrictive COVID-19 measures – fall squarely within his rights. These activities did not
“cause disturbances in public places ” or “disrupt social order ”, as alleged in the
Government’s response.
74. The Government accused Mr. Ji of spreading “false information”, without specifying
which content was deemed “false”. Instead, it explicitly cited his online expression as the
basis for his conviction. Neither Mr. Ji’s indictment nor the Government’s response provided
substantial or credible evidence to justify the charge of “picking quarrels and provoking
trouble”.
75. At the appeal hearing on 17 March 2024, Mr. Ji attempted to read a statement
disclosing the mistreatment he had endured in prison, but the judge interrupted him. A month
later, the court upheld his conviction.

A/HRC/WGAD/2025/9
 9
76. The source noted further abuses. When Mr. Ji protested against his mistreatment in
prison, officials retaliated with solitary confinement. His dental issues remain untreated,
forcing him to swallow food without chewing to avoid worsening his pain. The prison has
repeatedly denied Mr. Ji access to family visits, contra dicting claims made in the
Government’s response that the prisons have always guaranteed the rights of prisoners to life,
health, visits and correspondence. Neither Mr. Ji ’s family nor his lawyer ha ve received
responses to their letters.
77. In regard to Mr. Chen, the source recalls that he has spent over a year in pretrial
detention. His indictment clearly indicates that Mr. Chen is being prosecuted for posting a
compilation of video clips online, a peaceful act within his rights to free expression that does
not constitute the charge of “picking quarrels and provoking trouble ” as the Government
response alleged.
78. The Government claims that Mr. Chen ’s case is being delayed due to a  change of
defence lawyer. The source notes, however, that the delay in Mr. Chen’s case has, for a long
time, exceeded the period of three months prescribed by national law.
79. In addition, the source notes that the response failed to mention two critical procedural
issues: a pretrial hearing scheduled for 7 June 2024 was cancelled, with the court claiming it
needed more time, and another pretrial meeting on 16 August 2024 was held in violation of
domestic procedural rules , as the defen ce lawyers’ right to copy case files was obstructed.
Mr. Chen’s lawyers filed a complaint against the decision to deny the right of the defence
lawyers to review evidence. The court’s actions directly contradict the Government’s claims
of protecting Mr. Chen’s legitimate rights to a fair trial. To date, Mr.  Chen’s lawyers do not
have access to all the evidence listed in his indictment.
80. Furthermore, the source notes that the prison only allowed Mr. Chen outdoor time
once a month , and held him in an overcrowded cell forcing detainees to sleep sideways.
Under article 25 of the country’s Detention Cent re Regulations, detainees should have the
necessary sleep time and one to two hours of outdoor activity a day. Furthermore, according
to article 27 of the Implementation Measures of the Detention Cent re Regulations, the
average living space per detainee in a detention cell must not be less than two square metres.
Mr. Chen’s conditions in detention illustrate the opposite of the Government’s claim that the
country’s prisons have always enforced the law , adhering to strict, fair and civilized
standards. His access to outdoor time improved after his lawyer filed a complaint with the
Procuratorate.
 (d) Additional information from the source
81. On 7 January 2025, the source informed the Working Group that on the day before, 6
January 2025, a court in Shanghai had tried Mr. Chen and had sentenced him to three years
and six months in prison for “picking quarrels and provoking trouble”.
 2. Discussion
82. The Working Group thanks the source and the Government for their submissions. In
determining whether the deprivation of liberty of Mr. Ji and Mr. Chen is arbitrary, the
Working Group has regard to the principles established in its jurisprudence to deal wi th
evidentiary issues. If the source has established a prima facie case for breach of international
law constituting arbitrary detention, the burden of proof should be understood to rest upon
the Government if it wishes to refute the allegations. Mere assertions by the Government that
lawful procedures have been followed are not sufficient to rebut the source ’s allegations.3
83. The source has argued that the detention of Mr. Ji and Mr. Chen is arbitrary and falls
under categories II and III. The Working Group will proceed to examine these in turn.

A/HRC/WGAD/2025/9

 (a) Category I
84. Although the source has not explicitly framed its submission under category I, the
Working Group may examine issues ex officio  when the information provided suggests a
deprivation of liberty that lacks legal basis.
85. The Working Group notes that the source alleges that Mr. Ji was arrested on 31 August
2022 by officers from the Meiyuan New Village Police Station , which comes  under the
Pudong New District Branch of the Shanghai Public Security Bureau. When detaining Mr.
Ji, the police officers reportedly did not produce a warrant, in violation of article 83 of the
Criminal Procedure Law which stipulates that public security bu reau officers must produce
an arrest warrant when detaining an individual.
86. The Working Group recalls that anyone who is arrested is to be informed, at the time
of arrest, of the reasons for the arrest and is to be promptly informed of any charges. The
Working Group has previously stated that in order for a deprivation of liberty to have a legal
basis, it is not sufficient that there is a law which may authorize the arrest. The authorities
must invoke that legal basis and apply it to the circumstances of the case. 4 This is typically
done through an arrest warrant or arrest order (or equivalent document). 5 The right to be
presented with an arrest warrant is inherent to the right to liberty and security of person and
to the prohibition of arbitrary detention, under articles 3 and 9 of the Universal Declaration
of Human Rights as well as principles 2, 4 and 10 of the Body of Principles for the Protection
of All Persons under Any Form of Detention or Imprisonment.6
87. In the absence of any explanation from the Government in its reply to contradict these
allegations, the Working Group finds that Mr. Ji ’s arrest on 31 August 2022 was conducted
without legal basis, in violation of articles 3 and 9 of the Universal Declaration of Human
Rights.
88. Regarding Mr. Chen, the Working Group observes that similar concerns arise. The
source reports that Mr. Chen was arrested at his home in Shanghai on 28 November 2023 by
officials from the Baoshan Branch of the Shanghai Municipal Public Security Bureau and
was placed in criminal detention the following day. In the absence of specific information
showing that Mr. Chen was presented with a proper arrest warrant, the Working Group
concludes that his arrest also lack ed a proper legal basis , in violation of a rticles 3 and 9 of
the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
89. Furthermore, the Working Group observes that both Mr. Ji and Mr. Chen have been
charged under article 293 of the Criminal Law of China with “picking quarrels and provoking
trouble”. The Working Group has previously noted that this provision does not define with
sufficient precision what conduct amounts to “picking quarrels and provoking trouble ”. As
noted in its previous opinions, the Working Group considers that this provision is vague and
imprecise, allowing for the criminalization of conduct protecte d under international human
rights law.7 The determination of whether an offen ce has been committed appears to be left
entirely to the discretion of the authorities. The Working Group again emphasize s that
charges involving vague and imprecise offen ces jeopardize the ability of individuals to
exercise their fundamental rights and are likely to result in arbitrary deprivation of liberty.
90. The Working Group thus observes that both detainees were arrested, detained and
charged under vague provisions of the Criminal Law that fail to meet the principle of legality.
Considering the above, the Working Group concludes that the detention of Mr. Ji and Mr.
Chen lacks legal basis and is arbitrary, falling under category I.

 (b) Category II
91. The source submits that the detention of Mr. Ji and Mr. Chen constitutes a violation
of their rights to freedom of expression and assembly, including those guaranteed under
articles 18, 19 and 20 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
92. In the case of Mr. Ji, the Working Group notes that, according to the source, he was
detained primarily for his online criticism of the Government ’s COVID -19 pandemic
measures and for publishing open letters criticizing government officials. On 2 April 2022,
Mr. Ji posted a “citizen’s petition ” on WeChat and Twitter (now X), calling on the
Government to stop its restrictive pandemic measures. On 29 August 2022, Mr. Ji posted an
open letter on Twitter criticizing Shanghai ’s then  Party Secretary, who late r became the
Premier of China, call ing on him to step down and take accountability for the difficult
humanitarian situation caused by the lockdown.
93. The Working Group notes that these actions fall within the legitimate exercise of the
right to freedom of expression, as protected under article 19 of the Universal Declaration of
Human Rights. The Government has not demonstrated that Mr. Ji ’s expression posed any
threat to national security, public order, public health or morals, or the rights and freedoms
of others that would justify restricting his rights.
94. As regards Mr. Chen, the Working Group notes that, according to the source, he was
detained on 28 November 2023, just one day after he posted online a documentary video
about the “White Paper Protests” that had occurred in Shanghai on 26 November 2022. The
indictment against Mr. Chen specifically mentions his production and publication of this
documentary, which suggests that his detention is directly linked to his exercise of the right
to freedom of expression.
95. The Working Group notes that the right to freedom of expression includes the freedom
to seek, receive and impart information and ideas of all kinds, regardless of frontiers, either
orally, in writing or in print, in the form of art, or through any other media of one ’s choice.
The peaceful documentation and dissemination of information about protests falls within the
protection of the right to freedom of expression.
96. In the absence of a compelling explanation from the Government why restrictions on
their freedom of expression are justified, the Working Group concludes that Mr. Ji and
Mr. Chen have been deprived of their liberty for the peaceful exercise of their rights to
freedom of expression, in violation of article 19 of the Universal Declaration of Human
Rights. Their detention is therefore arbitrary, falling under category II of the Working Group.
 (c) Category III
97. The source argues that the detention of Mr. Ji and Mr. Chen also falls under
category III, due to the non -observance of international norms relating to the right to a fair
trial. Given its finding that the deprivation of liberty of Mr. Ji and Mr. Chen is arbitrary under
category II, the  Working Group emphasizes that no trial should have taken place.
Nevertheless, since the trials have taken place, the Working Group will examine the source’s
allegations.
98. In the case of Mr. Ji, the source reports that his lawyers experienced significant
obstacles in representing him effectively. The source alleges that authorities deprived Mr. Ji
of access to his legal counsel for longer than 48 hours after his request was made , which is
the limit set for a non-national security crime under article 39 of the Criminal Procedure Law.
In addition, during a visit on 26 April 2023, Mr. Ji ’s lawyer was reportedly not permitted to
read his case files, in violation of article 40 of the Criminal Procedure Law.
99. Regarding Mr. Chen, the source indicates that he was able to meet with a lawyer for
the first time one month after his apprehension, on 27 December 2023, and with his current
legal counsel on 8 February 2024. Moreover, the source submits that Mr. Chen ’s lawyers
have not been allowed to copy the electronic data from his mobile phone and computer, which
is being used as evidence against him. This data includes text, audio, and promotional video
materials, relevant to his defen ce. The Government did not re but these submissions  in its
reply.

12
100. The Working Group recalls that all persons deprived of their liberty have the right to
legal assistance by counsel of their choice at any time during their detention, including
immediately after their apprehension, and that such access must be provided without delay.
This right is essential for ensuring that the principle of equality of arms is observed in
criminal proceedings. The Government has failed to explain the restrictions placed on both
Mr. Ji’s and Mr. Chen’s access to legal assistance. The Working Group thus finds a violation
of articles 10 and 11 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
101. The Working Group further observes that Mr. Ji’s trial on 21 June 2023 was reportedly
closed to the public, with only two members of his family allowed to attend. Article 10 of the
Universal Declaration of Human Rights guarantees that “everyone is entitled in full equality
to a fair and public hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal ”. While the right to a
public hearing is not absolute, any restrictions must be strictly justified by considerations of
morals, public order or national security i n a democratic society. In the absence of such
justification from the Government, the Working Group finds that the restriction on the public
nature of Mr. Ji’s trial constitutes a violation of his right to a fair trial.
102. The source further alleges that during the trial, Mr. Ji was kept in handcuffs and forced
to sit in a cage behind metal bars, despite making numerous requests for the handcuffs to be
removed. Such presentation of the accused in court is incompatible with the presumption of
innocence guaranteed under article 11 (1) of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, as
it portrays the defendant as dangerous and likely guilty before any determination is made by
the court.
103. The Working Group notes with concern the source ’s allegation, not refuted by the
Government, that the materials Mr. Ji had prepared for his defen ce were confiscated by the
detention centre, and he was not allowed to bring them to court. Additionally, Mr. Ji was
reportedly only told about his hearing on the morning of the trial day, 21 June 2023, contrary
to national law requiring that trial summons be sent at least three days in advance.
104. Regarding Mr. Chen, the source notes that the authorities have repeatedly obstructed
access to case files by his legal defen ce team. Furthermore, his lawyers were not allowed to
copy electronic evidence that forms a critical part of the case against him, severely hampering
his ability to prepare an adequate defence.
105. These restrictions, not addressed by the Government in its reply, significantly impair
the ability of both individuals to prepare and present their defen ce, in violation of article 11
of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
106. The Working Group concludes that the above -mentioned violations of the right to a
fair trial are of such gravity as to give the deprivation of liberty of Mr. Ji and Mr. Chen an
arbitrary character. Their detention therefore falls under category III of the Working Group.
 (d) Category V
107. Although category V was not explicitly raised by the source, the Working Group has
found under category II that the detention of Mr. Ji and Mr. Chen resulted from their
legitimate exercise of freedom of expression. When a detention results from the active
exercise of civil and political rights, there is a strong presumption that the detention also
constitutes a violation of international law on the grounds of discrimination based on political
or other views. Accordingly, the Working Group will examine this category ex officio.
108. The Working Group notes that both Mr. Ji and Mr. Chen appear to have been targeted
due to their political opinions, particularly their criticism of government policies and
officials. In the case of Mr. Ji, his detention followed his criticism of the Government’s
COVID-19 pandemic measures and his calls for officials to be held accountable. For
Mr. Chen, his detention came immediately after he published a documentary about the
“White Paper Protests ”, which were demonstrations against the Government’s COVID-19
policies.
109. The authorities have , therefore, displayed an attitude towards them that can only be
characterized as discriminatory. In the absence of any explanation from the Government that
would refute this conclusion, and in the particular circumstances of th e present  case, the
Working Group finds that their detention violates articles 2 and 7 of the Universal Declaration

of Human Rights on the grounds of discrimination based on political or other opinion and is
arbitrary according to category V.
 3. Disposition
110. In the light of the foregoing, the Working Group renders the following opinion:
The deprivation of liberty of Ji Xiaolong and Chen Pinlin , being in contravention of
articles 2, 3, 7, 9, 11 and 19 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, is arbitrary
and falls within categories I, II, III and V.
111. The Working Group requests the Government of China to take the steps necessary to
remedy the situation of Mr. Ji and Mr. Chen without delay and bring it into conformity with
the relevant international norms, including those set out in the Universal Declar ation of
Human Rights.
112. The Working Group considers that, taking into account all the circumstances of the
case, the appropriate remedy would be to release Mr. Ji and Mr. Chen immediately and accord
them an enforceable right to compensation and other reparations, in accordance w ith
international law.
113. The Working Group urges the Government to ensure a full and independent
investigation of the circumstances surrounding the arbitrary deprivation of liberty of Mr. Ji
and Mr. Chen and to take appropriate measures against those responsible for the violation of
their rights.
114. The Working Group requests the Government to disseminate the present opinion
through all available means and as widely as possible.
 4. Follow-up procedure
115. In accordance with paragraph 20 of its methods of work, the Working Group requests
the source and the Government to provide it with information on action taken in follow -up
to the recommendations made in the present opinion, including:
 (a) Whether Mr. Ji and Mr. Chen have been released and, if so, on what dates;
 (b) Whether compensation or other reparations have been made to Mr. Ji and
Mr. Chen;
 (c) Whether an investigation has been conducted into the violation of the rights of
Mr. Ji and Mr. Chen and, if so, the outcome of the investigation;
 (d) Whether any legislative amendments or changes in practice have been made to
harmonize the laws and practices of China with its international obligations in line with the
present opinion;
 (e) Whether any other action has been taken to implement the present opinion.
116. The Government is invited to inform the Working Group of any difficulties it may
have encountered in implementing the recommendations made in the present opinion and
whether further technical assistance is required, for example through a visit by the Working
Group.
117. The Working Group requests the source and the Government to provide the
above-mentioned information within six months of the date of transmission of the present
opinion. However, the Working Group reserves the right to take its own action in follow -up
to the opinion if new concerns in relation to the case are brought to its attention. Such action
would enable the Working Group to inform the Human Rights Council of progress made in
implementing its recommendations, as well as of any failure to take action.
118. The Working Group recalls that the Human Rights Council has encouraged all States
to cooperate with the Working Group and has requested them to take account of its views
